title: Dancing Robot Car
pitch: A two-wheel robot that performs a programmed dance: spins, wiggles and a victory zoom.

guide.about: Learn how an H-bridge driver (the L298N) lets a weak board pin control strong motors: direction with IN1–IN4, speed with PWM on ENA/ENB. The motors get their own battery; the board only sends signals.
parts: plus 2 wheels and a chassis or a piece of cardboard
or any USB power for the board
wiring: swap them if it spins backwards
remove the 5V-EN jumper first: with 6V batteries the board powers the driver's logic
steps: Mount the two TT motors and wheels on a chassis (cardboard works!), plus a caster or a smooth bump at the front.
Screw the motor wires into OUT1/OUT2 (left) and OUT3/OUT4 (right).
Pull off the three jumpers: 5V-EN, ENA and ENB.
Wire the battery pack to 12V and GND on the L298N. Keep its switch OFF for now.
Connect L298N GND to board GND and L298N 5V to board 5V.
Wire ENA, IN1–IN4 and ENB to pins 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 6.
Upload the code with the robot lifted off the table, power the board, then switch the battery ON.
guide.test: After a 3-second countdown (the built-in LED blinks) the robot drives forward, spins left, spins right, wiggles, reverses and zooms. If a wheel turns the wrong way, swap that motor's two wires.
safety: Never power motors from board pins: the L298N and its own battery do that job.
The L298N heatsink can get warm. Don't touch it during long runs.
4×AA gives the motors only about 4V after the L298N's loss, so the robot is a bit slow. That's normal.
next: Add an ultrasonic sensor to dodge walls (see Obstacle-Dodging Robot).
Choreograph your own dance by editing the moves list.

title: Obstacle-Dodging Robot
pitch: A robot that drives around the room by itself and turns away when it sees a wall.

guide.about: Your first autonomous robot: it measures distance ahead, decides, and acts, about 20 times a second. That sense → think → act loop is how every robot works.
steps: Build the Dancing Robot Car first, or follow its motor wiring exactly.
Mount the ultrasonic sensor on the front, about 5 cm above the floor, facing forward.
Wire the sensor: VCC 5V, GND, TRIG Pin 11, ECHO Pin 12.
Upload the code with the wheels off the ground and check that both wheels spin forward.
Put it on the floor, switch on the battery, and step back!
guide.test: The robot drives forward. When something is closer than 25 cm it stops, backs up a little, turns in a random direction and continues. Adjust TURN_CM and the speeds in the code.
safety: Motors run only from the L298N and its battery, never from the board.
Keep fingers and hair away from the wheels when it's switched on.
next: Mount the sensor on a servo to look left and right before choosing a direction.
Add a bumper switch for objects the sensor misses.

title: Line-Following Racer
pitch: Draw a black track with electrical tape, and this robot races along it on its own.

guide.about: Two infrared sensors look down at the floor. If the left one sees the black line, the robot steers left; if the right one does, it steers right. The efficient TB6612FNG driver gives the motors more of the battery's power than an L298N.
parts: a mini breadboard on the chassis
steps: Solder header pins onto the TB6612FNG board and plug it into a mini breadboard on the chassis.
Mount the two line sensors at the front, facing down, about 1 cm above the floor and 2–3 cm apart.
Wire the driver, motors and battery exactly as in the table. All grounds must connect.
Wire the sensors' DO pins to Pin 2 (left) and Pin 3 (right).
Make a track: black electrical tape (about 2 cm wide) on a white floor or poster board.
Calibrate: hold each sensor over white, then black, and turn its screw until its LED is ON over white and OFF over black.
Upload, place the robot on the line, switch on the battery!
guide.test: The robot follows the line, correcting left and right. If it steers away from the line, swap LEFT/RIGHT sensor pins in the code or flip LINE_READS_HIGH.
safety: Motors are powered only through the TB6612FNG from the batteries, never from board pins.
Soldering: hot iron, use the stand, ventilate.
next: Add a third sensor in the middle for smoother steering.
Time your laps with a TM1637 stopwatch.

title: Knob-Speed Desk Fan
pitch: A little desk fan whose speed you set with a knob, switched safely with a MOSFET.

guide.about: A logic-level MOSFET is a strong electronic switch: the board's pin only touches its gate, while the motor current flows from the battery. A flyback diode protects everything from the voltage spike a motor makes when switched off.
parts: plus a small propeller (often sold with it)
wiring: MOSFET Gate (left pin, label facing you)
keeps the fan off while the board boots
silver stripe toward Battery +, other end on the Drain side
steps: Place the MOSFET in the breadboard with its printed label facing you: pins are Gate, Drain, Source from left to right.
Gate: 220Ω to Pin 9, plus 10kΩ from Gate to GND.
Source to GND. Connect the battery pack's − to the same GND.
Motor: one wire to Battery +, the other to the Drain.
Put the 1N4007 diode across the two motor wires with the silver stripe on the Battery + side. Backwards = short circuit!
Wire the potentiometer to 5V, GND and A0.
Upload, switch the battery on and turn the knob.
guide.test: The fan is off at one end of the knob and speeds up smoothly as you turn. The Serial Monitor (9600) shows the speed in %.
safety: Double-check the diode direction before switching on: the stripe goes to Battery +.
Keep fingers away from the spinning propeller.
The MOSFET stays cool with this small motor; if it gets hot, check your wiring.
next: Add a DHT11 so the fan switches on automatically when it's hot.
Use a bigger 5V fan with a separate 5V supply.

title: Auto Plant Waterer
pitch: When the soil gets dry, a tiny pump gives your plant a drink by itself. Perfect for holidays.

guide.about: Combine a soil sensor with a MOSFET-switched pump. The code waters in short bursts, then waits for the water to soak in before measuring again, so it can't flood the pot.
wiring: through 220Ω, plus 10kΩ from Gate to GND
stripe (−) to GND: smooths the pump's start-up
steps: Calibrate the soil sensor first (see the Thirsty Plant Alert guide) and write your DRY_VALUE and WET_VALUE into the code.
Build the MOSFET switch: Gate via 220Ω to Pin 7, 10kΩ Gate→GND, Source to GND.
Pump red wire to 5V, black wire to the Drain. Diode across the pump with the stripe to 5V.
Add the 100µF capacitor across 5V and GND (stripe/− side to GND).
Put the pump in a water container that sits LOWER than the plant, and run the tube to the pot.
Power the board from a 2A USB charger, upload, and watch the Serial Monitor (9600).
guide.test: When moisture drops below 35%, the pump runs for 3 seconds, then waits 60 seconds before checking again. It never runs more than 5 times in a row (a safety limit in case the sensor falls out).
safety: Keep the board, breadboard and charger far away from water; only the pump goes in the container.
Never connect the pump straight to a board pin: the MOSFET + diode protect the board.
Test with a cup of water in a sink first.
next: Add a water-level sensor to warn when the tank is empty.
Use an ESP32 and get a phone notification after each watering.

title: Silent Haptic Metronome
pitch: A metronome you feel instead of hear: a buzz on every beat, with a knob for 40–200 BPM.

guide.about: Musicians use haptic metronomes to practice silently. A transistor switches the little vibration motor from the 5V pin, and PWM at about 60% keeps the motor's average voltage near its rated 3V. The first beat of each bar buzzes longer.
parts: check its pin order (E-B-C or C-B-E) in the datasheet
wiring: the code limits it to ~3V average with PWM
steps: Find your transistor's pins from its datasheet (search the number printed on it): Emitter, Base, Collector.
Base through 1kΩ to Pin 9, Emitter to GND.
Motor red wire to the board's 5V pin, motor's other wire to the Collector.
Diode across the motor, stripe toward 5V.
Potentiometer to 5V, GND and A0. Optional LED on Pin 13.
Upload and turn the knob to set the tempo.
guide.test: The motor buzzes on every beat: long on beat 1, short on beats 2–4. The Serial Monitor (9600) shows the BPM.
safety: Never power the vibration motor from a board pin: the transistor handles its ~80mA.
If the transistor gets hot, its pins are probably swapped. Unplug and re-check the datasheet.
next: Add a TM1637 to show the BPM.
Add a button for 3/4 and 6/8 time.

title: Gamer Macro Pad
pitch: Four big buttons that type keyboard shortcuts on your PC: copy, paste, undo and screenshot, or your game's hotkeys.

guide.about: The Leonardo can pretend to be a USB keyboard. Each button sends a key combination, and you can change them to anything your games or apps use.
steps: Wire each button between its pin and GND (arcade buttons: use the COM and NO tabs).
Install the Keyboard library if the IDE asks for it.
Upload the code with Board set to Arduino Leonardo.
Open Notepad, select some text and try the buttons.
Change the shortcuts in the sendShortcut() function, e.g. to your game's skill keys.
guide.test: Button 1 copies (Ctrl+C), 2 pastes (Ctrl+V), 3 undoes (Ctrl+Z), 4 opens the Windows snipping tool (Win+Shift+S).
safety: A board that types by itself can do surprising things: the code only sends keys when you press a button, and waits 3 seconds after plugging in.
next: Add a rotary encoder for volume up/down.
Put it in a 3D-printed or cardboard case.

title: Joystick Mouse
pitch: Control your PC's mouse pointer with a thumb stick. Click by pressing the stick down.

guide.about: The Leonardo acts as a USB mouse. Joystick tilt becomes pointer speed (with a "dead zone" in the middle so it doesn't drift).
steps: Wire the joystick: GND, +5V to 5V, VRx A0, VRy A1, SW Pin 2.
Upload with Board set to Arduino Leonardo.
The mouse control starts switched OFF. Click the stick once to turn it on.
Tilt to move, click to left-click. Hold the stick down for 2 seconds to switch mouse control off again.
guide.test: After enabling, tilting moves the pointer: a little tilt = slow, full tilt = fast. Letting go stops it.
safety: Mouse control starts disabled, so a wiring mistake can't send your pointer flying.
next: Add a second button for right-click.
Use an MPU-6050 instead for a tilt-mouse.

title: Touch Glow Light
pitch: A tiny night light: tap a touch pad to change colors, hold it to dim. Thumb-sized and gift-ready.

guide.about: A TTP223 touch pad tells the ESP32-C3 when you tap or hold it, and an 8-LED stick shows soft colors. Brightness is capped so it runs happily from any USB charger.
wiring: through 330Ω. 3.3V data works on this short wire; a level shifter (74AHCT125) makes it bulletproof
steps: Solder header pins to the LED stick if needed.
Install the Adafruit NeoPixel library.
Wire the touch pad to 3V3, GND and GPIO 3.
Wire the stick: 5V, GND, and DIN through a 330Ω resistor to GPIO 4.
In Tools set Board: ESP32C3 Dev Module and USB CDC On Boot: Enabled, then upload.
Tap to change color, hold to dim.
guide.test: Each tap switches between warm white, pink, mint, purple, amber and off. Holding the pad slowly dims the light; release to keep that level.
safety: Soldering: hot iron, use the stand and ventilate.
next: Put it inside a frosted jar or a 3D-printed anime-figure base.
Add Wi-Fi control from your phone.

title: Wi-Fi Signal Meter
pitch: A pocket meter that shows your Wi-Fi strength as a bar. Find the best spot for your router or gaming setup.

guide.about: The ESP32-C3 scans for your network every second and draws its signal strength on a slim OLED. Walk around with a power bank to map dead zones.
steps: Install Adafruit SSD1306 and Adafruit GFX Library.
Wire the OLED: VCC 3V3, GND, SDA GPIO 5, SCL GPIO 6.
Put your Wi-Fi name in TARGET_SSID (no password needed, it only listens). Leave it empty to show the strongest network.
Set Board: ESP32C3 Dev Module, USB CDC On Boot: Enabled, then upload.
Walk around: the bar shows the signal.
guide.test: The OLED shows the network name, a bar and the dBm value. -50 is excellent, -70 is OK, -80 is weak.
next: Beep faster where the signal is stronger: a Wi-Fi metal detector!
Log the best spot's value.

title: Rainbow Status Light
pitch: The ESP32-S3 has a tiny RGB LED built in. Make it breathe rainbow colors, or type a color name to set it.

guide.about: No parts needed. The DevKitC-1 has an addressable RGB LED on board. You'll drive it with rgbLedWrite() and read commands from the Serial Monitor.
parts: USB-C, plugged into the UART port
steps: Choose Tools → Board → ESP32S3 Dev Module.
Plug into the port labeled UART (or COM).
Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 (Newline).
Watch the rainbow, then type red, green, blue, pink, white, off or rainbow and press Enter.
If the LED stays dark, your board version uses GPIO 38: change RGB_PIN to 38.
guide.test: The small LED near the USB ports cycles smoothly through the rainbow, and your typed colors switch it instantly.
next: Show Wi-Fi status: blue while connecting, green when connected.
Flash red when a sensor value is too high.

title: ESP32-S3 Macro Keyboard
pitch: The S3's native USB turns 4 buttons into a real USB keyboard. Shortcuts for gaming, streaming or homework.

guide.about: Unlike classic ESP32s, the S3 has real USB built in, so it can act as a keyboard just like an Arduino Leonardo. This uses the S3's "USB-OTG (TinyUSB)" mode.
steps: Wire each button between its GPIO and GND.
In Tools set Board: ESP32S3 Dev Module and USB Mode: USB-OTG (TinyUSB).
Upload through the port labeled UART.
Now also connect the port labeled USB to your PC. This is the keyboard.
Press the buttons in any app.
guide.test: Windows shows a new keyboard. Buttons send Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+M (mute in Teams/Discord-style apps) and Win+Shift+S.
safety: Keys are only sent when you press a button, so the board can't type by itself.
next: Add an OLED that shows the current layer of shortcuts.
Add a rotary encoder for volume.

title: Wi-Fi Camera Stream
pitch: Watch a live video from the ESP32-CAM on your phone's browser. Pet cam, plant time-lapse or robot eye!

guide.about: The ESP32-CAM grabs JPEG frames from its camera and streams them over Wi-Fi as an "MJPEG" video that any browser can show. Programming needs the ESP32-CAM-MB USB board (usually sold together).
parts: micro-USB for the ESP32-CAM-MB programmer board
a solid 2A charger avoids brownout resets
wiring: press it on: the pins only fit one way
steps: Make sure the camera ribbon is clicked in, then press the ESP32-CAM onto the MB programmer board.
In Tools choose Board: AI Thinker ESP32-CAM.
Type your Wi-Fi name and password into the code.
Upload. If it says "Failed to connect", hold the IO0 button on the MB board, press RST, release IO0 and upload again.
Press RST to run, then open the Serial Monitor at 115200 to see the IP address.
Open that address on your phone (same Wi-Fi) to watch the stream.
guide.test: The page shows live video at about 5–15 frames per second. Only one viewer at a time.
safety: Anyone on your Wi-Fi can open the stream. Don't point it at private spaces.
Brownout resets mean weak power: use a good 5V 2A supply.
Your Wi-Fi password is stored in the code.
next: Add a button that saves a photo to the microSD card.
Mount it on the robot car for first-person driving.

title: Color Memory Challenge
pitch: Watch the lights flash a pattern, then repeat it. Each round adds one more step. How long can you go?

guide.about: A classic memory game. Each color has its own tone, the sequence is stored in an array, and the game checks every press. Great practice for arrays and game states.
parts: four 220Ω for LEDs + one 220Ω for the buzzer
steps: Place the 4 LEDs in a row with a button below each one.
Wire each LED with its 220Ω resistor to pins 8–11, and each button to pins 2–5 (other legs to GND).
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 12.
Upload. All lights blink: press any button to start.
Watch, listen, repeat!
guide.test: Round 1 flashes one color, round 2 adds another, and so on. A wrong press plays a sad sound and shows your score in the Serial Monitor (9600).
next: Speed up the flashes every 5 rounds.
Show the score on a TM1637 display.

title: Whack-a-LED
pitch: LEDs pop up at random. Smack the matching button before they vanish! 30 seconds, how many can you hit?

guide.about: A speed game with 3 "moles". The time each LED stays lit shrinks as your score grows. Uses millis() to run a 30-second round without blocking.
steps: Place the 3 LEDs in a row with a button in front of each.
Wire LEDs (with 220Ω) to pins 9, 10, 11 and buttons to pins 2, 3, 4.
(Optional) Buzzer through 220Ω on Pin 8.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Press any button to start a 30-second round.
guide.test: A random LED lights; hitting its button scores a point (high beep), the wrong button costs a point. After 30 s all LEDs flash and your score prints.
next: Use arcade buttons in a cardboard box for a real arcade cabinet.
Add a high-score that survives power-off (EEPROM).
